doc.title: Sheryl Bailey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 24, 2023

chapter: Women in jazz and the business
title: Guitar in studio work, hard to replace electronically; pedals
summary: They discuss why guitar resists synthesis in scoring and Bailey's pedal use with Anat Cohen.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Another quote from Sheryl. I recently interviewed a number of musicians who mostly made their life in the studios, some of them going way back and a lot of them point out that that part of the business has changed so much and a lot of the studio work is disappearing because it can be replaced. And I wonder if you — I hadn’t even thought about this until this morning actually, that the guitar I think is the hardest instrument to replace electronically or synthesizer-wise. There’s something about it and maybe it’s more immune to the technology than other instruments that can be easily re-created now.

That might be true. I mean I think there’s some great scoring of guitar in some of the TV shows that — it’s all guitar-generated stuff and different sounds, and definitely, because you know if you’re talking about film scoring you could have a scene in a honky tonk, you could have a scene in a jazz club, you could have — you know I mean there are so many places, an acoustic guitar, could be flamencos kind of sound. Yeah, it’s not reproducible in an electronic way that’s convincing.
Yeah. There’s something about the strumming and it’s just hard to reproduce that. If I went to a jazz club in New York that you were playing at would I see a lot of foot pedals or things to stomp on?

It depends. If you saw me with Anat Cohen yes, because I have to do my big flame- thrower solo at the end. Yeah I mean I use certain things because sometimes I have some tunes that might have a certain vibe. Most of the time I go for a clean sound but you know I always like to have some options.
